page.title: Correspondence Matrices: a structural layer for Boolean computation

domains.lede: Boolean logic is the arithmetic of yes and no. It looks trivial in isolation — an AND, an OR, a NOT — and becomes hard the moment you have thousands of them wired together and need a guaranteed answer about all of their combinations at once. That situation is far more common than it sounds.
lay: A Boolean expression is a rule built from conditions that are each either true or false: this user is an admin AND the account is not suspended. Evaluating it once, for one specific case, is easy. The hard questions are about all possible cases: is there any combination of inputs that lets this through? Do these two rules always agree? Which condition is actually doing the work?

Those questions are hard because the number of combinations doubles with every condition you add. Twenty conditions is a million cases; forty is a trillion. Every field below has some version of this problem, and each has built its own tools for it.
technical: Each domain below is a place where the central object is a Boolean function over a set of variables and the question of interest is a property of the whole function rather than a single evaluation: satisfiability, equivalence, implicant structure, reachability, or minimal representation. The representations differ; the underlying algebra does not.

These are candidate application domains for a structural layer, not validated deployments of this one. No result on this site was measured on a workload from any of them apart from the EPFL circuits, which sit under formal verification and hardware synthesis.

items.name: AI reasoning and neuro-symbolic systems
items.question: Given everything the model has concluded so far, is this next step even consistent?
items.lay: Systems that mix learned prediction with hard rules need a way to check that a proposed answer does not violate the rules — and to do it fast enough to sit inside a reasoning loop.
items.technical: Constraint propagation and consistency checking over a symbolic knowledge layer, typically with heavy reuse of the same constraint set across many candidate assignments.
items.lay_name: AI that mixes learning with hard rules

items.name: Formal verification and EDA
items.question: Are these two circuits the same circuit?
items.lay: Before a chip design is manufactured, engineers must prove that the optimised version computes exactly the same thing as the original — for every possible input, not just the ones they tested.
items.technical: Combinational equivalence checking, model checking, and property verification. This is the domain that produced BDDs, and the one the external validation on this site draws its circuits from.

items.name: Constraint solving and SAT
items.question: Is there any way to satisfy all of these requirements at once?
items.lay: Scheduling, planning, packing, routing: enormous numbers of interlocking yes/no choices where you need one workable combination, or proof that none exists.
items.technical: Boolean satisfiability over CNF, with modern conflict-driven clause-learning solvers. The question is existential rather than exhaustive, which is why SAT scales to problems where explicit enumeration cannot.

items.name: Hardware design and synthesis
items.question: What is the smallest set of gates that computes this function?
items.lay: Turning a description of what a circuit should do into an actual arrangement of gates, using as little silicon and power as possible.
items.technical: Logic synthesis, technology mapping, and two-level or multi-level minimisation. Representation choice directly determines what optimisations are even expressible.

items.name: Rule engines and decision systems
items.question: Which rule fired, and why?
items.lay: Insurance pricing, credit decisions, benefits eligibility, medical triage protocols: large bodies of business rules that must produce an explainable decision and must not contradict each other.
items.technical: Decision tables and rule networks where the operational needs are conflict detection, redundancy elimination, coverage analysis, and traceable attribution of an outcome to a rule.

items.name: Security policy and access control
items.question: Can any user reach this resource by some path we did not intend?
items.lay: Permission systems are Boolean expressions over roles, attributes and context. The dangerous question is not what a policy does allow but what it accidentally allows.
items.technical: Policy analysis over role and attribute predicates: reachability, privilege-escalation search, policy-difference computation between two versions, and change-impact analysis.

items.name: Configuration and feature flags
items.question: Is this combination of settings even reachable, and what does it do?
items.lay: A product with forty independent switches has more than a trillion possible configurations. Teams need to know which combinations are valid, which are dead, and what a new flag interacts with.
items.technical: Configuration-space analysis over feature models: dead-feature detection, constraint consistency, and repeated evaluation of the same predicate under many different flag assignments.

items.name: Computational biology and Boolean networks
items.question: Which stable states can this regulatory network settle into?
items.lay: Gene regulation can be modelled as switches turning each other on and off. Researchers want the long-run states the system falls into, and what perturbations move it between them.
items.technical: Boolean network dynamics: attractor identification, basin-of-attraction analysis, and control-target search over networks of Boolean update functions.

items.name: Knowledge graphs and ontologies
items.question: Does this new fact contradict anything already asserted?
items.lay: Structured knowledge bases carry rules about what can and cannot be true together. Adding facts means re-checking consistency, constantly.
items.technical: Consistency and subsumption checking over description-logic constraints, where the same constraint structure is re-queried under many different partial assignments.

items.name: Compiler optimisation and program analysis
items.question: Can this branch ever be taken?
items.lay: Compilers reason about which conditions can hold at each point in a program, so they can delete impossible branches and prove that a rewrite is safe.
items.technical: Path-condition reasoning, dataflow analysis, and reachability over predicates — with repeated partial evaluation of the same condition under evolving context, which is exactly the reuse pattern a compiled structural representation would target.

toolbox.lede: Each tool below is excellent at the thing it was built for and mediocre or irrelevant at the others. There is no honest single speed ranking across them, because they do not produce the same thing.
lay: Compare a calculator, a spreadsheet, and a proof. All three deal with numbers. Asking which is fastest is a malformed question — they produce different outputs and answer different questions. The Boolean toolbox is in the same position.

The useful question is not “which is best?” but “what am I actually asking for?” If you want a specific answer, you want something that computes it. If you want a guarantee that covers every case at once, you want something that reduces the rule to a standard shape, or a solver. If you want the smallest circuit, you want a minimiser.
technical: Grouped by role: execution kernels produce an explicit output vector over the semantic support (BitSet, the CM packed path, compiled evaluators). Symbolic engines produce a graph or normal form that supports post-construction queries (ROBDD/CUDD, SAT, SymPy). Minimisers produce a smaller equivalent expression (Espresso).

A comparison is only meaningful within a role, and only when both sides produced the same artifact — which is why every timed comparison in this project is gated on bit-for-bit output equality first, and why construction and evaluation costs are never merged into one ranking.

tools.name: BitSet (packed explicit evaluation)
tools.question: What is the complete answer table for this expression?
tools.superpower: Almost no overhead. It packs many input combinations into machine words and evaluates them all in parallel with ordinary bitwise instructions. Nothing to build, nothing to look up.
tools.cost: The output is exponential in the number of variables that matter. It has no reusable structure — ask again tomorrow and it does the same work again.
tools.analogy: A very fast pocket calculator. No setup, no memory, brilliant for one-off sums.
tools.measured: The fastest end-to-end path at every semantic support measured here, from {{wrap.k4.median}} faster at live_k=4 down to {{wrap.k16.median}} at the guard limit.
tools.lay_question: What is the answer for every possible combination of inputs?

tools.name: ROBDD / CUDD
tools.question: Are these two functions the same? Can I query this function repeatedly without re-deriving it?
tools.superpower: Reduces a function to a canonical graph. Under a fixed variable order, two functions are identical exactly when their graphs are identical — so equivalence becomes a pointer comparison.
tools.cost: The graph's size depends heavily on the variable ordering, and finding a good order is a search with a real price. Pulling an explicit answer table back out is expensive, because it means walking the graph once per combination.
tools.analogy: A well-organised index. Expensive to build and sensitive to how you sort it, but then any lookup is instant.
tools.measured: Built the whole corpus in {{cudd.build.min_us}}–{{cudd.build.max_us}} into graphs of {{cudd.nodes.k16}} nodes or fewer — while full extraction of the explicit vector ran {{cudd.extract.min_x}}–{{cudd.extract.max_x}} slower than the packed kernels.
tools.lay_question: Are these two rules the same — and can I keep asking questions about one of them cheaply?

tools.name: SAT solver
tools.question: Is there any assignment that satisfies all of this?
tools.superpower: Finds one satisfying answer, or proves none exists, on problems with millions of clauses — without ever enumerating the space.
tools.cost: Answers an existence question, not an enumeration question. It will not hand you the full answer table, and counting solutions is a different and much harder problem.
tools.analogy: A search party. Superb at finding one thing in an enormous space; the wrong tool for mapping the whole space.
tools.measured: Not benchmarked in this project. It answers a different question from anything measured here, and no comparison against it is claimed.
tools.lay_question: Is there any combination at all that satisfies all of this?

tools.name: Espresso
tools.question: What is the smallest two-level form of this function?
tools.superpower: Heuristic minimisation that reliably produces compact sum-of-products covers, which is what a hardware synthesis flow wants next.
tools.cost: Optimises expression size, not evaluation speed, and targets a specific two-level form rather than arbitrary structure.
tools.analogy: An editor who cuts your draft in half without changing what it says.
tools.measured: Not benchmarked in this project. It optimises a different objective from anything measured here.
tools.lay_question: What is the shortest way to write this rule?

tools.name: SymPy (symbolic algebra)
tools.question: Can I manipulate this expression algebraically — simplify it, substitute into it, transform it?
tools.superpower: General-purpose symbolic manipulation with a very wide vocabulary of transformations, well beyond Boolean logic.
tools.cost: Generality has a price. It is not built for packed evaluation and is orders of magnitude off the pace of a dedicated kernel on that task.
tools.analogy: A full mathematics workbench. Everything is possible; nothing is optimised for one job.
tools.lay_question: Can I rearrange this expression the way I would rearrange algebra on paper?

tools.name: Structural CSE (+ sharing-aware flattening)
tools.question: If I compile this expression to a shared graph and evaluate that, how fast is it?
tools.superpower: Identifies repeated subexpressions, computes each once, and — with sharing-aware flattening — collapses chains of the same operator into single wide operations without duplicating shared work.
tools.cost: Preparation is not free, and the compiled program only pays off if you evaluate it more than once.
tools.analogy: Doing your working out on paper once and then reading off the answers, instead of redoing the arithmetic each time.
tools.measured: This is the baseline the whole project is measured against. Against a plain CSE with no flattening, CM runs about {{kernel.local.pct}} faster. Against sharing-aware CSE-flat, B1/E3 and EPFL measured parity, while current B2/B4 V3 measured bare CM at {{symv3.bare.overall}} overall and {{symv3.bare.k16}} at k=16.
tools.lay_question: If I do the working-out once and keep it, how fast is it after that?

tools.name: CM (Correspondence Matrices)
tools.question: What operator produced this? How is it structured? Can it be transformed, decomposed, cached, or matched against another?
tools.superpower: Treats the operator itself as the object. It gives every expression a canonical key, keeps a persistent compiled cache, serialises, and knows which variables actually matter before it evaluates anything.
tools.cost: Compilation costs roughly {{prep.min}}–{{prep.max}} what the CSE baseline's does, and the end-to-end call carries {{wrap.ovh.min}}–{{wrap.ovh.max}} of fixed overhead. Both must be amortised by reuse.
tools.analogy: A build system rather than a compiler. The value is in knowing what you already built and being able to reuse it — not in the raw speed of any single build.
tools.measured: Workload-dependent against CSE-flat: parity on B1/E3 and EPFL, but a modest bare-program advantage on current B2/B4 V3. The public wrapper was still {{symv3.wrapper.overall}} [{{symv3.wrapper.overall.lo}}, {{symv3.wrapper.overall.hi}}] overall, so no end-to-end speed moat is established. Structural keys, caching, and serialisation remain separate differentiators.
tools.lay_question: Have I seen this rule before, what is it made of, and can I store it and reuse it?

whatIsCM.lede: A Correspondence Matrix represents a Boolean operator as an ordered binary matrix. The point is not that it computes a different answer — it computes exactly the same answer — but that it makes a different set of operations expressible.

lay: A truth table answers what are the outputs? You list every combination of inputs and write down what comes out. It is complete, and for a fixed variable ordering it pins the function down exactly.

A Correspondence Matrix answers a different question: what operator produced those outputs, and what is its structure? Same function, same answers — but now the operator is an object you can hold, compare, decompose, and store.
technical: A complete truth function, a normalised CM, and a reduced ordered BDD can each identify a Boolean function under their respective conventions. Their organisation and their supported operations differ. Uniqueness of a CM is relative to an ordered variable basis; matrix equality requires the same normalised ordered basis on both sides.
This is the same distinction as between a list of a function's values and a closed-form expression for it. Both determine the function; only one supports algebraic manipulation.

lay: Here is the single most important idea for reading any chart on this site. Suppose a system has 32 variables available, and you write the expression x2 AND x17.

Two variables matter. The other thirty do not appear and cannot change the answer. The meaningful output is four rows — every combination of two variables. The ambient truth table over all 32 variables has 4,294,967,296 rows, but 4,294,967,292 of them are copies of those same four answers.

So the honest measure of how big a job is is not how many variables exist. It is how many variables actually change the answer. This project calls that number live_k, and it is the horizontal axis of essentially every chart here.
technical: Nominal n is the size of the variable namespace. Syntactically used variables are those appearing in the expression. Semantic support, live_k, counts variables with a genuine functional effect — a variable can appear syntactically and still be semantically dead, as in x AND (y OR NOT y).

Explicit output size is 2live_k, not 2n. Plotting against nominal n without qualifying semantic support silently compares shallow sparse formulas against dense all-live ones and produces curves that mean nothing.
This is not a modelling assumption; it was measured. Holding live_k fixed and varying the ambient namespace across {{b4.ambient_ns}} moves the measured ratio by {{b4.k16.spread}}.

operatorCalculus.lede: Representing an operator as a matrix makes a family of operations expressible that a truth table does not naturally support. It is important to be exact about which of those are implemented, which exist in the formalism but have never been demonstrated on a workload, and which are neither.

The formalism supports those questions. That is a genuine and separate claim from “we have implemented them and shown they pay off,” and this project has been careful not to blur the two.

scenarios.lede: This is the part that should actually change what you do. Each scenario below is a shape of problem, a recommendation, and the measurement that supports it.

items.question: I need to evaluate one expression, once.
items.verdictWhy: there is no setup to spread across
lay: If you are going to ask a question once and then move on, you want the tool with the least setup. BitSet has essentially none: it loads many input combinations side by side into the chunks of memory the processor works in, and works out all their answers in a single pass.

CM has to compile the expression first, look it up in its store of already-compiled work, plug in your inputs, and read the result back out. All of that is real work, and if you only evaluate once there is nothing to spread it across. At the smallest problems the setup costs several times more than the actual computation.
technical: The measured end-to-end ratio favours BitSet at every semantic support tested, from {{wrap.k4.median}} at live_k=4 to {{wrap.k16.median}} at live_k={{wrap.max_k}} — and that is the cached case, where the CM program is already compiled. Uncached in a warm environment the ratio runs {{wrap.uncached.min}}–{{wrap.uncached.max}}.

The gap is fixed overhead, not kernel speed: {{wrap.ovh.min}}–{{wrap.ovh.max}} of binding, environment setup, cache lookup and extraction per call. Because it is roughly constant, it shrinks in relative terms as the useful work grows — at live_k={{wrap.max_k}} the bare BitSet call is already {{wrap.k16.bitset_us}} against a CM call of {{wrap.k16.cm_us}} — but it does not vanish below the guard limit.

The corresponding pre-repair claim that CM was modestly ahead at controlled live_k 12 and 16 does not survive this measurement. It is listed in the corrections ledger and appears nowhere else on this site.

items.lay_question: I need to answer one question, once.

items.question: I need to evaluate the same expression thousands of times.
items.verdict: It depends entirely on how many times — and you should measure that first
items.verdictWhy: reuse count is the decision variable
lay: Now the calculus changes. Compilation is a one-time cost, and each evaluation afterwards is slightly cheaper. So there is some number of evaluations at which compiling pays for itself. Below it you lose; above it you win.

That break-even number is the single most useful thing to know about your workload. Against a plain, unflattened baseline the typical synthetic expression needs about {{be.syn.median}} evaluations, and the typical real circuit about {{be.epfl.median.matched}} — worse, but not by a lot.

Against a properly flattened baseline, break-even depends on the workload. On the EPFL AND/INV workload each evaluation was effectively tied, so there was nothing to accumulate and {{be.epfl.never}} of {{be.epfl.total}} real circuits were marked “never.” Current B2/B4 V3 instead measured a bare CM/CSE-flat ratio of {{symv3.bare.overall}}, but its public wrapper ratio was {{symv3.wrapper.overall}}; any new break-even claim must therefore include preparation and the exact wrapper boundary rather than extrapolate from the bare kernel.
So the honest advice is not “use CM for repeated evaluation.” It is: work out what you are really comparing against, then work out how many times you will actually re-evaluate.
technical: Break-even is the preparation premium divided by the per-evaluation kernel gain. A formula is classified as never breaking even exactly when that gain is not positive — preparation cost sets the magnitude of the finite counts but plays no part in the classification.

Baselines must be matched before any two of these figures are compared. Against plain CSE: synthetic median {{be.syn.median}} with {{be.syn.never}} of {{be.syn.total}} never, prep {{be.syn.prep}}; EPFL median {{be.epfl.median.matched}} with {{be.epflcse.never}} of {{be.epfl.total}} never, prep {{be.epflcse.prep}}. Against CSE-flat on EPFL: median {{be.epfl.median}} with {{be.epfl.never}} of {{be.epfl.total}} never ({{be.epfl.never_pct}}), prep {{be.epfl.prep}}. The synthetic-versus-plain-CSE figure and the EPFL-versus-CSE-flat figure are not a like-for-like pair and are never quoted as one.
The distributions are right-skewed with a substantial never-break-even mass in every arm, which is why the median alone is a poor summary and the histogram is shown.

Because break-even is a ratio of two small timings it moves with ordinary run-to-run variation, as does the preparation multiple. The archived run of the same synthetic corpus reports slightly different values for both; the discrepancy is recorded in section 6 under “Open discrepancies between the summary prose and the raw evidence”, and the workload-dependence conclusion is identical either way. The headline kernel ratio, by contrast, is stable across the two runs.

items.lay_question: I need to answer the same question thousands of times.

items.question: My expressions have very few live variables — or quite a lot.
items.verdict: The right evaluation engine changes with the workload, not at a fixed variable count
items.verdictWhy: and a rule based on variable count alone gets it wrong
lay: There are several ways to actually compute the answer bits. One walks the expression recursively. One flattens it first and works over big integers. One packs bits into machine words and processes them in blocks.

The word-packed engine is the fastest of the three when there is enough work to do — but it pays a fixed setup cost on every call. On the expressions measured here that cost is not repaid until a fairly large number of variables matter, and below that the simple flattened approach wins by a wide margin.

The practical lesson is that a rule of the form “switch engines above six variables” is not safe. What matters is how much work there is to pack, which depends on the shape of the expression and not just on how many variables matter.
technical: Flat big-integer evaluation beats the recursive kernel at every support measured, with ratios of {{bx1.fvr.min}}–{{bx1.fvr.max}}. That part is unconditional.

The word-packed engine's fixed dispatch cost keeps flat fastest through live_k={{bx1.last_flat_k}} on this corpus; words only wins at live_k={{bx1.first_words_k}}, at {{bx1.k16.wvf}} of flat. At live_k=6 — where a support-only rule would have switched — words is {{bx1.k6.wvf}} slower than flat.

Restate the rule as an amortisation condition: word-packed evaluation wins when the packed work, roughly 2<sup>live_k</sup> words times the operation count, is large enough to absorb the fixed dispatch cost. Deck-era corpora with larger operation counts genuinely did cross at smaller supports. Both statements are corpus-scoped; neither is a universal threshold. A validated backend selector is listed as open work for exactly this reason.

Above live_k={{guard.k}} the explicit path declines rather than producing an output that doubles in size with each further variable. Across {{guard.trials}} fresh trials the guard made {{guard.wrong}} wrong decisions and let through {{guard.oversized}} oversized outputs.
items.lay_verdict: Measure it; do not use a rule of thumb
items.lay_verdictWhy: the fastest choice shifts with the work, not the variable count
items.lay_question: Only a few of my inputs actually change the answer — or a great many do.

items.question: I need a canonical form, an equivalence check, or a compact symbolic object.
items.verdictWhy: and do not ask it for an explicit answer table
lay: If your real question is “are these two things the same?” or “can I keep asking questions about this rule cheaply?”, you want a standard shape. A decision diagram gives you one: build both rules the same way, testing the inputs in the same sequence, and they are the same rule exactly when the two diagrams come out identical. No need to check every case.

CUDD is excellent at this, and on the expressions measured here it is cheap to build. But asking it to hand back the complete answer table is asking it to do the one thing its whole structure exists to avoid — it has to walk the diagram once for every combination, and the number of combinations doubles with each variable you add.
So this is not a contest CUDD loses. It is two different jobs, and the numbers below are the price of converting between them.
technical: Construction and evaluation are reported as separate panels and are never combined into a single ranking, because they produce different artifacts. Construction: {{cudd.build.min_us}}–{{cudd.build.max_us}} including fresh-manager creation and variable declaration, yielding graphs of {{cudd.nodes.k16}} nodes or fewer.

Full extraction of the packed vector ran {{cudd.extract.min_x}}–{{cudd.extract.max_x}} slower than the packed kernels ({{cudd.kernel.min_us}}–{{cudd.kernel.max_us}}), reaching {{cudd.extract.k16_ms}} at live_k=16. The growth is structural: extraction is linear in 2<sup>live_k</sup> assignments.

The comparison is like-for-like: robdd_is_cudd held on all {{cudd.rows}} rows and CUDD's full extraction matched the CM packed bits exactly on every one, so both sides genuinely produced the same answer.

Variable ordering is a real cost centre. Trying ten seeded orders and keeping the smallest graph gave {{bx2.node_saving.min_pct}}–{{bx2.node_saving.max_pct}} fewer nodes at about {{bx2.search_x.min}}–{{bx2.search_x.max}} the single-build cost. CUDD's dynamic reordering never triggered at {{bx2.max_nodes}} nodes and below — its node ratio is exactly {{bx2.reorder_ratio}} — which says this corpus is small for CUDD, not that reordering is ineffective.
items.lay_verdictWhy: just don't ask it for the full answer table
items.lay_question: I need to prove two rules are the same, or ask lots of questions about one rule.

items.question: My workload is real circuits, not generated formulas.
items.verdict: Expect a tie against a well-built compiled baseline
items.verdictWhy: the external validation is the strongest evidence here
lay: Everything above could have been an artifact of the formula generator. So the project took a published benchmark suite of real hardware circuits it had never measured against, wrote down in advance what result would count as meaningful, and ran it.

The answer: against a carelessly built competitor CM is genuinely faster — about {{kernel.epfl.pct}}. Against a carefully built one the two came out level, with the measured difference smaller than the uncertainty in the measurement itself.
That is the honest headline. CM's case does not rest on being quicker than a well-built competitor at the computation itself, and this measurement is what settled it.
technical: {{epfl.n_cones}} AND/INV combinational cones extracted from {{epfl.n_circuits}} circuits in the EPFL suite ({{epfl.n_aig_files}} AIG files, upstream commit {{epfl.clone_commit}}, corpus SHA-256 {{epfl.corpus_sha}}). Confidence intervals are circuit-clustered, because cones from the same circuit are not independent observations.
Primary arm CM ÷ CSE-flat: {{flat.epfl}} [{{flat.epfl.lo}}, {{flat.epfl.hi}}]. Secondary arm CM ÷ plain CSE: {{kernel.epfl}} [{{kernel.epfl.lo}}, {{kernel.epfl.hi}}].

The mechanism check is what makes “kernel-equivalent” a claim rather than a shrug. CM's advantage over a plain CSE comes from merging chains of the same operator into single wide instructions. On AND/INV circuits every gate is binary, so flattening has already captured everything there is to merge — and the instruction-count and executed-operation ratios against CSE-flat are both exactly {{mech.instr_ratio}}. The mechanism predicted parity on this corpus, and parity is what was measured.
The cost side is worse on real circuits than on synthetic ones: preparation {{be.epfl.prep}}, and {{be.epfl.never}} of {{be.epfl.total}} cones never break even against CSE-flat.

frontier.lede: The 2026-08-03 campaign established parity against CSE-flat on B1/E3 and EPFL. The accepted 2026-08-25 V3 correction narrowed that conclusion: current B2/B4 measured a workload-specific bare CM advantage, while the public wrapper remained slower. Three fresh same-host repetitions ranged from {{symv3.repeat.min}} to {{symv3.repeat.max}}, confirming the direction while exposing run-level variation that a within-run formula interval cannot measure. A later three-pod preparation confirmation passed, while a genuinely held-out i10 feature selector failed and the simple k=16 rule transferred well. The remaining questions are therefore about preparation, boundary cost, reuse, and choosing by workload rather than declaring one universal kernel ratio.
lay: It is worth being clear about what kind of problem is left. “Is CM faster?” has no workload-free answer: B1/E3 and EPFL measured parity at the kernel, current B2/B4 V3 measured a modest bare CM lead, and the public wrapper remained slower. The remaining questions are about total cost, choosing, and capabilities that exist on paper but have never been shown to pay.

Three of them are cheap to answer and would move the picture immediately. Three more are the experiments that would actually test whether the structural idea is worth anything beyond re-running the same expression. Two are engineering and formal gaps. And two are honest boundary questions — regions the measurements simply do not cover.

The preparation replication and first untouched selector transfer test are now complete. The next useful work is narrower: real reuse traces, another independently frozen selector family, and dependency-gated native comparators where the workload justifies them.
technical: The B1/E3 CM-versus-CSE-flat residual remains below its pre-registered materiality bar and is not an optimisation target. V3's separate B2/B4 bare-program result is accepted as workload-specific, not universal. Optimisation priority remains preparation cost, cache behaviour, wrapper economics, and workload-aware backend selection.

Several items below are marked partially answered. That means a preliminary experiment exists and produced a result — often a negative or CM-versus-CM one — that does not meet the success criterion the project wrote for it. Those are reported as they stand rather than upgraded by optimism.

items.title: No real deployed workload has ever been measured
items.lay_statement: Everything here answers “how many times would you have to re-run this before compiling pays off?” Nobody has yet gone and measured how many times real systems actually do re-run the same expression. Without that number, the economics stay hypothetical in both directions.
items.technical_statement: This is distinct from what the external validation delivered. The EPFL campaign supplied real circuit cones and validated kernel ratios and the structure of the preparation and break-even economics on real expressions — but it measured per-formula kernel and preparation costs, not an application's actual reuse distribution or end-to-end task cost. The ranked next test is a reuse-distribution measurement on a real consumer workload, to calibrate expected reuse against predicted break-even. The candidate validation domains named by the project remain untested as workloads: configuration and policy systems, hardware verification and EDA, compiler and program analysis, and constraint satisfaction in AI systems.
items.why_it_matters: Reuse count is the decision variable for the entire cost argument. Every recommendation in section 4 that says “it depends how many times” is waiting on this measurement.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: If it succeeds — a measured reuse distribution with typical reuse well above the measured break-even — CM's economics convert from “depends on your workload” into a quantified applicability statement, and the selector gets its calibration data. If it fails — a distribution concentrated below break-even — real systems do not reuse compiled expressions often enough for the preparation multiple to amortise, and CM becomes a correct structural layer with no cost argument on real workloads.
sources: deliverables_n22_24/CM_GAP_EPFL_VALIDATION_2026-08-03.md — scope of what the external campaign did and did not measure
items.downside: If real systems turn out to re-evaluate rarely, the setup premium never amortises in practice — CM becomes a correct structural layer with no cost argument on real workloads at all.

items.title: Preparation is profiled — and remains the top optimisation surface
items.lay_statement: Before CM can answer anything it does a one-time setup step costing roughly {{prep.min}}–{{prep.max}} what the simple alternative's setup costs. The deep audit traced that work and removed one redundant compilation memo safely. That improvement then reproduced on {{memo.pods}} Linux machines; a more ambitious compact-ordering idea was exact but much slower and was removed.
items.technical_statement: Preparation costs {{be.syn.prep}} plain-CSE prep on the synthetic corpus, {{be.epflcse.prep}} on the external corpus against the same baseline, and {{be.epfl.prep}} against CSE-flat, with a per-case range of {{b3.prep_ratio.min}}–{{b3.prep_ratio.max}} across the compile-scaling cases. The 2026-08-25 deep audit measured a distributed profile led by interning, lowering, live-support work, structural hashing, rewrite, and canonicalisation. It removed the redundant identity memo only from the sharing-aware builder path, with exact ordered-DAG and packed-output gates. Three independent Runpod CPU flavors then measured candidate/baseline preparation at {{memo.bx1b2.min}}–{{memo.bx1b2.max}} on BX1+B2 and {{memo.epfl.min}}–{{memo.epfl.max}} on EPFL, with {{memo.mismatches}} exact mismatches, cost {{memo.cost}}, and {{memo.postflight_pods}} postflight pods. The subsequent exact rational compact-order prototype preserved all {{dpr1.rows}} smoke outputs but cost {{dpr1.time}} time and {{dpr1.peak}} traced peak memory; it was rejected and reverted.
items.why_it_matters: Break-even is the preparation premium divided by the per-evaluation kernel gain, so preparation sets how large every finite break-even count is. Halving it roughly halves those counts and widens the band of workloads where compiling pays. It does not, however, rescue the never-break-even population — a formula is classified “never” exactly when the per-evaluation gain is not positive, which is a property of the comparison, not of the setup cost.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: The small one-memo improvement is now cross-host confirmed. Any further preparation change needs a different measured mechanism from the rejected compact-order prototype, paired exact evidence on representative and high-sharing cases, and benefit large enough to repay compatibility and maintenance risk.
sources: deliverables_n22_24/CM_GAP_POST_ACCEPTANCE_OPTIMIZATION_DECISION_2026-08-03.md §7 ranked next tests, item 3; §8 ranked optimizations, item 1
items.downside: If the cost is spread thinly across several stages with no dominant one, the setup premium is intrinsic to building a reusable, storable structure — and CM is a high-reuse-only layer whose case rests entirely on what it stores, not on cost.

items.title: The persistent cache has never been studied
items.lay_statement: One of the three things CM is left standing on is that it remembers what it has already compiled. Nobody has measured how often that memory actually helps under a realistic mix of work, or how sensitive it is to how much you let it remember.
items.technical_statement: The persistent cache is named as the second optimisation surface, with cache-policy tuning as a ranked optimisation gated on the study existing. The only recorded production characteristic to date is incidental: the cache returns one object per digest, which is what keeps a known duplicated-slot behaviour narrow in practice — it requires mid-compile eviction or deliberate cross-builder mixing. Everything else is unmeasured: steady-state hit rate, working-set size, eviction policy, invalidation correctness when an expression changes, memory retention, and cold-versus-warm cost.
items.why_it_matters: Without a universal kernel advantage, the cache is one of the remaining potential differentiators. An unmeasured differentiator is an architectural assertion.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: If it succeeds — measured hit rates and a sensitivity curve for the cache size limit under realistic mixes — cache-policy tuning gains a quantified payoff and the differentiator gains empirical content. If it fails — low hit rates or high sensitivity to the size limit — the cache is a fragile differentiator, the duplicated-slot behaviour stops being exotic, and the amortisation argument weakens further on top of an already-substantial preparation cost.
items.downside: If hit rates are low or highly sensitive to how much is retained, one of the three remaining differentiators is fragile, and the amortisation argument weakens on top of an already-substantial setup cost.

items.title: The simple k=16 rule transferred; a richer feature selector did not
items.lay_statement: CM has several internal engines. The old switch at six variables was badly wrong, so the implementation moved to a conservative switch at sixteen. On a new circuit that simple rule stayed close to the best engine. A more complicated rule trained on the old data looked plausible there but made many disastrous choices on the new circuit, so it was rejected.
items.technical_statement: The older rule — big-integer evaluation below six live variables, word-packed at six and above — remains rejected: flat big-integer beat the recursive kernel at every support ({{bx1.fvr.min}}–{{bx1.fvr.max}}), stayed fastest through live_k={{bx1.last_flat_k}}, and words won only at live_k={{bx1.first_words_k}}; at k=6 words was {{bx1.k6.wvf}} slower. The current k=16 control then transferred to {{i10.rows}} untouched Berkeley ABC i10 cones spanning k={{i10.min_k}}–{{i10.max_k}}, with raw and CM regret {{i10.current.raw}} and {{i10.current.cm}} and zero catastrophic routes. A preregistered ridge selector trained only on BX1 features failed the same held-out gate: regret {{i10.feature.raw}} raw and {{i10.feature.cm}} CM, with {{i10.feature.raw.cat}} and {{i10.feature.cm.cat}} catastrophic routes. It was rejected without retuning on i10. No production feature selector is integrated.
items.why_it_matters: Selection is where “different tools answer different questions” becomes an engineering deliverable rather than a slogan. Getting it wrong costs multiples silently. And a selector that cannot be shown to generalise out of sample is indistinguishable from a rule overfitted to the two corpora this project happens to own.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: A replacement must first clear its tuning-corpus cross-validation catastrophe gate, then beat k=16 on another independently frozen circuit family without using i10 for tuning. Until then the honest response is to keep the simple documented threshold and treat richer automatic routing as rejected research, not a shipped advantage.
items.downside: If a fitted rule does not transfer to data it was not fitted on, it is overfitted to the two test sets this project owns, and any “automatic routing” language has to narrow to the simple policy already shipped.

items.title: Canonical CM equivalence exists in the formalism and nowhere else
items.lay_statement: CM's most distinctive claim is that two differently written expressions can be recognised as the same object by their structure. In practice the project has only ever checked that two things produce the same answers. Matching answers is required for sameness — it does not prove it.
items.technical_statement: The current path establishes output equality, including full 2live_k packed equality against CUDD on all {{cudd.rows}} matched rows. None of that is a canonical CM-equivalence proof. Matrix equality requires the same normalised ordered basis; a truth table, a normalised CM and a reduced ordered BDD each identify a Boolean function under their own conventions, and none of those conventions is interchangeable with the others. What CM does have is compact interned canonical keys, resting on a documented hash-collision assumption, with one interned twin per builder — which is an engineering property, not a promise of global object identity, and the project's own clarifications say so.
items.why_it_matters: This is the capability that would distinguish CM from “a structural IR with a good cache”. Without it, the differentiator list reduces to keys, caching and serialisation — all real, all reproducible by other means.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: If it succeeds — a defined normal form with proven invariants, exhaustive validation over small Boolean functions and bases, and canonicalisation-cost and artifact-size figures comparable to ROBDDs — “canonical keys” becomes a defensible formal claim. If it fails, the negative result is still worth having: it would pin down that CM canonicality depends on arbitrary basis and order choices, fix the public language permanently at “output-based equivalence”, and force the prior question the project has not answered — whether the canonical artifact offers anything that ROBDDs, AIG normalisation or canonical truth representations do not already supply.
sources: CM slide deck, frozen at Audit V4 (2026-07-24), not in-repo — “CM Equivalence Caveat” and “Basis-Normalized Representation” slides; framing quoted, never its numbers
items.downside: If no workable normal form exists, CM's most distinctive claim stays informal permanently, the public language is fixed at “same answers” rather than “same object”, and the prior question — what this buys over existing canonical forms — becomes unavoidable.

items.title: Cross-expression and related-family reuse — preliminary, and it has not beaten the real baseline
items.lay_statement: If you evaluate a whole family of closely related expressions — successive versions of a policy, revisions of a circuit — CM ought to be able to reuse work between them. A first experiment showed it reusing work compared with a version of itself that had no cache. It has never been shown to beat the actual competitor.
items.technical_statement: The project's own success criterion is that CM's preparation cost amortises across the family and that total family cost falls below repeated BitSet evaluation. Current state: a cross-expression subtree-cache implementation improved cached CM against uncached CM on shared-block cases, with mixed results on composition mixes, while BitSet remained faster by more than an order of magnitude in the strongest exact-output cases cited. A CM-versus-uncached-CM improvement is not the comparison the criterion names. The retest guidance is explicit: do not re-run the existing synthetic family sweep; use real edit, version and query families, and compare against hash-consed DAGs, e-graphs, incremental BDD managers and compiler memoisation as well as uncached CM.
items.why_it_matters: This is the workload shape a structural layer is supposed to be for. If it does not pay here, the persistent cache's story collapses back to “re-run the same compiled formula many times”, and the family and versioning domains — policy versions, circuit revisions, compiler passes — drop out of scope.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: Question: does CM's structural IR reduce cost when evaluating a family of related expressions? Success: preparation amortised across the family with total family cost below repeated BitSet evaluation, under fair total-cost accounting — the first demonstration that the structural layer buys something on a workload shape BitSet cannot exploit. Failure: structural reuse does not generalise beyond same-expression prepared evaluation, and the honest claim narrows to a scoped same-expression preparation cache.
sources: CM slide deck (frozen at V4), “Three CM-Value Experiments” card 1 and priority experiment 04 — framing only
items.downside: If reuse does not generalise past re-running one identical expression, the caching story collapses to exactly that, and the versioning and family use cases — policy revisions, circuit revisions, compiler passes — drop out of scope.

items.title: Repeated partial contexts — tested, and CM lost
items.lay_statement: Many real systems evaluate the same rule over and over with most of the inputs held fixed and a few varying. CM should be able to keep the fixed part's work. When this was tested, CM did beat a version of itself with no cache — and still lost to both BitSet and to the decision-diagram approach at every size tried.
items.technical_statement: Success criterion: CM partial evaluation faster than full re-evaluation for repeated partial contexts. Current state: partially tested with a negative comparative result. Cached CM improved substantially over uncached CM, and in one fixed-fraction sweep by a larger factor still — but BitSet and ROBDD restriction remained faster throughout the tested range. The retest guidance calls for real context traces (sliding, random, locality-heavy, adversarially low-overlap, phase-changing) compared against CUDD restrict/cofactor and incremental SAT with assumptions, and asks for a break-even surface over original support, remaining live support, number of contexts, context overlap, output type, cache budget, and cold versus steady state — not a single ratio.
items.why_it_matters: Combined with the already-measured BitSet lead at every semantic support up to the guard, a second negative result here would mean the structural layer offers no execution-time advantage on incremental workloads either — and the value proposition would have to rest entirely on the artifacts rather than on time.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: Question: does CM preserve reusable structure across related variable assignments? Success: established on real traces against CUDD restrict/cofactor and incremental SAT — not merely against uncached CM — this gives CM a defensible operational niche independent of raw kernel speed, and populates the break-even surface the selector needs. Failure: partial-context reuse provides no measurable advantage over BitSet.
sources: CM slide deck (frozen at V4), “Three CM-Value Experiments” card 2 and priority experiment 05 — framing only
items.downside: If incremental workloads show no advantage either, then combined with the already-measured loss at the whole-call boundary, the structural layer offers no execution-time advantage anywhere, and the case must rest entirely on stored artifacts.

items.title: Operator difference and quotient — implemented and correct, practical value unproven
items.lay_statement: The formalism lets you ask structural questions about operators themselves: what is the difference between these two rules, can this one be factored. Those operations have been implemented and shown to be correct. Nobody has yet shown a real task where using them is cheaper or better than the obvious alternative.
items.technical_statement: Directional quotienting, transpose, complement, rotations, operand swap, expression negation and operand-negation transforms are implemented and validated. The measured comparison is where care is needed: BitSet was faster for the semantic-delta task, and CM's quotient computes a different artifact — it is not a faster semantic XOR. The project records this as a standing anti-pattern: never benchmark the quotient as though it were a semantic-difference speed contest, because that compares two different outputs. This sits squarely in the formalism column: the artifact is a structural operator representation, and its practical performance advantage has not been benchmarked.
items.why_it_matters: This is the only capability on the list that could not be reproduced by bolting CSE plus flattening onto an existing evaluator. If it never demonstrates value, the operator calculus remains a correct but unused feature and CM's public claim reduces to a well-engineered structural IR with a well-tested explicit-output path.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: Question: do CM-native transformations produce practical workload value? Success: lower measured total cost than a clearly specified baseline, or a formally defined operator result whose practical value is demonstrated on a representative workload — this would be a capability claim rather than a speed claim. Failure: CM-native transformations provide no measurable advantage for this workload type.
sources: CM slide deck (frozen at V4), “Three CM-Value Experiments” card 3 — framing only
items.downside: If no task is found where the operator transformations are cheaper or better, the formalism stays a correct but unused feature and the public claim reduces to a well-engineered structural representation with a well-tested output path.

items.title: The decision-diagram comparison has only been run where ordering barely matters
items.lay_statement: The order in which a decision diagram tests its variables can change its size dramatically — for some functions, catastrophically. The expressions measured here are all easy in that respect, so the comparison against decision diagrams has been made only in the region where their hardest failure mode never appears.
items.technical_statement: The order-search question is closed with data: best-of-ten order search yielded {{bx2.node_saving.min_pct}}–{{bx2.node_saving.max_pct}} smaller graphs at {{bx2.search_x.min}}–{{bx2.search_x.max}} the single-build cost, and dynamic reordering never triggered — node ratio exactly {{bx2.reorder_ratio}} — because at {{bx2.max_nodes}} nodes and below the trigger threshold is never reached. That last fact is the limitation. What remains open is a controlled study over standard parameterised families with known behaviour — easy and reducible, parity-like, multiplexer, arithmetic and circuit-derived, and deliberately order-sensitive — reporting for each: fixed order, explicitly stated alternative orders, best-of-k with the full search cost, the dynamic-reordering method and its total cost, and node count, peak memory, build time and each downstream query kept separate.
items.why_it_matters: Comparing a packed evaluator against decision diagrams only on diagram-friendly inputs risks reading a favourable extraction ratio as a general property. On genuinely hard families the packed path may become infeasible before the diagram does.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: If it succeeds — a controlled sweep across friendly, hard and order-sensitive families with search and reordering costs quoted separately — the result is a defensible boundary atlas showing where each representation is feasible at all. If it goes against CM — diagram compactness holds on hard families while the packed path becomes infeasible because the explicit output is exponential in live support — the honest conclusion is that CM's operating region is strictly bounded by explicit-output size, and every comparison here must be scoped to workloads where a packed truth vector is the required artifact.
sources: CM slide deck (frozen at V4), ongoing caveats — framing only
items.downside: If decision diagrams stay compact on genuinely hard functions while the explicit-output path becomes infeasible, CM's operating region is strictly bounded by output size, and every comparison here must be scoped to workloads where an explicit answer table is what you actually need.

items.title: Above the guard limit, bounded kernels work but the public boundary still refuses
items.lay_statement: The system refuses to produce an explicit answer table above sixteen live variables, because the table doubles in size with every variable after that. A bounded follow-up did run the underlying exact kernels from {{guard.followup.min_k}} through {{guard.followup.max_k}}: all {{guard.followup.cases}} cases completed with {{guard.followup.mismatches}} wrong answers and {{guard.followup.timeouts}} timeouts. The public wrapper still refused every case, so this proves a small feasibility band, not permission to raise the limit or a CM speed win.
items.technical_statement: The original guard remains correct: {{guard.wrong}} wrong decisions and {{guard.oversized}} oversized outputs across {{guard.trials}} earlier trials. The bounded subprocess follow-up then exercised exact direct kernels for live_k={{guard.followup.min_k}}–{{guard.followup.max_k}} under a 64 MiB estimate cap, 512 MiB RSS cap, 45-second timeout and three repetitions: {{guard.followup.cases}}/{{guard.followup.cases}} completed, with {{guard.followup.mismatches}} mismatches, {{guard.followup.timeouts}} timeouts and {{guard.followup.wrapper_non_refusals}} wrapper non-refusals. This closes the claim that nothing above the guard has been measured, but it did not compare equivalent whole-call CM and BitSet artifacts or justify a production policy change.
items.why_it_matters: The evidence now separates three facts: bounded direct kernels are feasible just above the line, complete output still grows exponentially, and the supported public API intentionally refuses that region.
items.what_would_change_the_picture: A caller-backed, memory-safe study would need equivalent whole-call artifacts, paired CM/BitSet timings, retained and temporary memory, and a pre-allocated refusal policy. Only then could the public guard be reconsidered; a direct-kernel feasibility result alone is insufficient.
items.downside: Every additional live variable doubles complete-output size. Extending the sweep without a caller, equivalent artifact boundary, and hard memory protocol would spend resources without supporting a production decision.

discipline.lede: Each of these exists because breaking it produced a wrong published number at some point in this project's history.

rules.rule: Nothing is timed until both sides agree, bit for bit
rules.lay_explanation: Before the stopwatch starts, every method being compared has to produce exactly the same answer — every bit identical. If two methods disagree, that is a bug to fix, not a data point to quietly drop. Otherwise you can measure something fast that is simply computing the wrong thing.
rules.technical_explanation: Packed-equality gating across every arm and the wrapper, on every formula, before any timing is recorded. For the decision-diagram comparison this was strengthened from sampled checks to full extraction equality on all {{cudd.rows}} rows, so the timed comparison is provably of the same answer produced two ways. Compile-scaling cases likewise verified packed equality across all arms on every case.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: A faster implementation that is subtly wrong looks like a win. Worse, an arm that fails on hard inputs and succeeds on easy ones gets timed only on the easy ones, which is survivorship bias dressed as a speedup.

rules.rule: The pass mark for the decisive experiment was written down before the data existed
rules.lay_explanation: The most important measurement in the project had its success threshold fixed in advance, in a document, before anyone had a single external number. Then the experiment ran — and failed to meet the threshold. The project reported that and changed its claim, rather than looking for another way to slice the data.
rules.technical_explanation: The external protocol pre-registered the corpus source, cone-selection rules, arms, schedules, clustering basis and a three-condition materiality rule: the external CM ÷ CSE-flat geometric mean had to be at or below 0.95, and its circuit-clustered interval had to exclude parity, and the median break-even had to be at or below 1000. The measured result was {{flat.epfl}} [{{flat.epfl.lo}}, {{flat.epfl.hi}}] — the first two conditions failed. That failure makes parity the final posture for the EPFL AND/INV workload. The later B2/B4 V3 result is reported separately and rules out silently generalising that posture to every workload.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Without a threshold fixed in advance, any result can be narrated as a success. Pre-registration is what makes a negative result informative instead of merely disappointing.

rules.rule: Confidence intervals are clustered on the right unit
rules.lay_explanation: If you time the same expression seven times, you have not measured seven expressions — you have measured one, seven times. Treating those as seven independent facts makes your error bars look far tighter than they are. Every interval on this site is built by resampling the thing that is actually independent.
rules.technical_explanation: The inferential unit is the formula, the cell, the source circuit, or the machine — never the timing round. The synthetic corpus uses a stratified-by-cell bootstrap; the external corpus uses a circuit-clustered bootstrap, because {{epfl.n_cones}} cones come from only {{epfl.n_circuits}} circuits and cones from one circuit share structure; machines are reported individually and never pooled. Circuit clustering makes the external interval wider than a cone-level interval would be, and that width is the honest one.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Pseudo-replication. Repeated rounds inflate the effective sample size, intervals shrink toward zero width, and a difference that is well within run-to-run noise acquires the appearance of statistical significance.

rules.rule: The two measurement orders are reported separately and never averaged
rules.lay_explanation: You can time one method fully and then the other, or you can alternate between them. Those two orders leave the computer's fast temporary memory in different states, so they are genuinely two different measurements. Reporting only their average hides which one you did — so both are always shown.
rules.technical_explanation: Blocked and round-robin schedules are reported as separate columns wherever both are measured, and are never pooled into a single figure. The campaigns that measure both are the corrected kernel experiment, its replay, the cross-machine replication and the external validation. The wrapper-boundary, guard, engine-crossover and order-sensitivity runs are blocked-only and say so on their reports.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: An earlier pass in this project attributed a schedule effect to a real performance difference. Once the two orders were separated the effect was visible as what it was. Pooling would have hidden it permanently.

rules.rule: Every summary number is recomputed from the raw rows by someone other than the code that produced it
rules.lay_explanation: The program that runs a benchmark also prints a summary. That summary is not trusted. A separate program re-reads the individual measurements and recomputes every headline figure from scratch, and the two have to match before anything is published.
rules.technical_explanation: Independent reaggregation from the raw per-formula rows precedes citation of any statistic. The corrected kernel experiment was reaggregated by a third-party pass in which every summary row reproduced to within floating-point tolerance, break-even reproduced exactly on all formulas, and all stratified intervals agreed. This page does the same thing again: every figure here is recomputed by the build script from the raw evidence files, never copied from a report's prose.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: A bug in the summarising code becomes a published result. Two separate passes in this project's history found exactly that.

rules.lay_explanation: The set of test expressions is fixed and given a short fingerprint derived from its exact contents. Every machine that runs the benchmark re-checks that fingerprint first. If one character changed, the run stops. So when five machines report different timings, you know it is the machines that differ and not the questions they were asked.
rules.technical_explanation: Corpora carry SHA-256 digests recorded in the campaign manifest and verified at each point of use. The cross-machine replication verified the corpus digest on every machine and additionally required the identity fields of every row to match exactly. The external corpus's upstream source is pinned to a specific commit with per-file digests and a licence digest recorded.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Silent corpus drift. Two runs disagree and there is no way to tell whether the workload or the machine changed.

rules.rule: Every timing is labelled with what it actually includes
rules.lay_explanation: “How long did it take?” is ambiguous. Did that include building the compiled program, or not? Did it include getting the answer back out? Every number here says which, because comparing a figure that includes setup against one that does not is the easiest way to publish a wrong ratio.
rules.technical_explanation: Timings are typed: preparation, kernel, end-to-end call, extraction, and — for decision diagrams — build, sampled evaluation and full extraction, each reported separately. The build window convention is stated explicitly wherever two runs use different ones: the matched comparison's build includes creating a fresh manager and declaring variables, while the order-sensitivity run's build is expression-to-diagram conversion only. Those two are never plotted on the same axis.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: A superseded wrapper-overhead figure in this project's history was carried forward from a different corpus and timing protocol without re-measurement, and understated the real cost by a large factor.

rules.rule: Only matched pairs are aggregated, and every refusal is recorded
rules.lay_explanation: If one method manages a hard case and the other gives up, that pair cannot be averaged into a speed comparison — you would be crediting one method for the cases where its competitor was absent. Only cases where both methods answered are counted, and every case where one declined is reported separately.
rules.technical_explanation: Failure-aware paired reporting: unmatched observations are excluded from ratio aggregation, and skips, guard trips and runtime refusals are counted and published rather than dropped. The external campaign reported {{epfl.n_cones}} of {{epfl.n_cones}} rows successful with zero runtime-guard skips; the guard sweep reports the decline rate for every cell alongside the timings.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Survivorship bias. The arm that fails more often on hard inputs is measured only on easy ones and appears faster than it is.

rules.rule: Building a thing and using a thing are never merged into one ranking
rules.lay_explanation: Some tools spend effort up front to make later questions cheap; others do no setup and pay on every question. Adding those two costs into a single “speed” number produces a ranking that is meaningless for both. They are always shown as separate panels.
rules.technical_explanation: Construction cost and evaluation or extraction cost are measured, reported and plotted as distinct quantities. There is no three-way winner anywhere on this site, and there is deliberately no blended ranking across tools that produce different primary artifacts.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: A canonical-form engine looks terrible at a job it was never designed for, or an evaluator looks free because its setup was charged to a different column.

rules.rule: The workload axis is live_k, not how many variables exist
rules.lay_explanation: How big a job is depends on how many things actually matter, not on how many things are lying around. Charts plotted against the total number of variables silently mix easy sparse problems with hard dense ones and produce curves that mean nothing.
rules.technical_explanation: Semantic support is measured, not assumed, and is the horizontal axis of every chart here with one stated exception: the guard chart, whose question — how often is a randomly drawn expression from a namespace of this size declined — is genuinely about the namespace. The axis choice was itself verified: holding semantic support fixed while varying the ambient namespace across {{b4.ambient_ns}} moves the ratio by {{b4.k16.spread}}, and on that chart nominal n appears as the series rather than the axis.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Shallow sparse formulas and all-live formulas get compared as if they were the same size of problem, and any resulting scaling curve is an artifact of the mix.

rules.rule: Withdrawn numbers are named, not deleted
rules.lay_explanation: When a published figure turns out to be wrong, it is listed in a standing correction table alongside the reason it was wrong and what replaced it — rather than quietly disappearing. Anyone who read the old material can find out exactly what changed.
rules.technical_explanation: A standing erratum and claim map name every superseded figure with its status — confirmed, revised, or superseded — and its replacement. On this site those figures appear in exactly one place, the corrections ledger, struck through, and are never plotted. Where the summary prose and the raw evidence still disagree, that disagreement is published too rather than resolved silently in favour of the nicer number.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Superseded figures leak back into later material because nobody recorded that they were withdrawn. This has happened in the project's history and is what the ledger exists to prevent.

rules.rule: Reproduce a reported finding before fixing it — and be willing to refute it
rules.lay_explanation: When an outside reviewer reports a problem, the first step is to reproduce it independently, not to fix it. Several reported problems turned out to be real; at least one turned out to be wrong, and was recorded as refuted rather than fixed to be agreeable.
rules.technical_explanation: Externally reported findings are independently reproduced before any change is made, and are refuted where the evidence does not support them. In the consolidated corrective pass, six of seven external findings were confirmed and addressed and one was refuted on the evidence. A separate formal argument about decision-diagram size was refuted as stated while its practical conclusion was upheld — the exact bound in the argument was wrong, and node counts do not imply byte size or runtime, but the practical conclusion it supported survived.
rules.what_goes_wrong_without_it: Agreeableness masquerading as rigour. Fixing a non-problem adds risk and hides the fact that the reviewer's model was wrong.

chain.stage: Audit V2 — review of unreviewed third-party changes
chain.what_was_checked: Whether a set of externally contributed changes should be kept, and whether seven associated claims held up.
chain.outcome: All third-party changes kept. A real fairness bug was confirmed: a large-namespace flag was being applied asymmetrically between the arms, so published ratios at larger namespaces were not like-for-like and were superseded.

chain.stage: Audit V3 — adversarial review, then an independent review of that review
chain.what_was_checked: Seven findings about evaluator correctness, variance estimation, generator structure and engine parity — then all seven re-checked by a separate pass.
chain.outcome: All seven findings confirmed, including one that refuted a prior claim rather than supporting it. Several survived only with narrower wording. Latent gaps identified in the same pass were fixed.

chain.stage: Audit V4 — latent-fix verification and three matched comparisons
chain.what_was_checked: Whether the V3 fixes were correct within their stated blast radius, plus three honest head-to-head comparisons including native decision-diagram construction.
chain.outcome: All fixes confirmed correct with no production mismatch. This is the state the slide deck is frozen at — and the state most of whose measured numbers the 2026-08-03 campaign has since superseded.

chain.stage: Gap audit — adversarial review of the benchmark gap analysis
chain.what_was_checked: Corpus construction, compilation risk, formula-level replication, schedule labelling, survivorship, and the fairness of the baseline.
chain.outcome: Directionally right on every count, and it exposed that the controlled strata were built from a single formula each — so the inferential unit was one, not seven.

chain.stage: Deep follow-up — audit of both the gap analysis and the gap audit
chain.what_was_checked: Whether the two preceding documents were themselves correct.
chain.outcome: Both contained load-bearing errors. The decisive new defect: an instruction count was being used as an executed-operation count, which is not the same thing — and flattening duplicates shared work, so a naive flattened baseline was doing more work than it needed to. That is the finding that eventually retracted the largest headline in the project.

chain.stage: Gap repair — production repair, then an adversarial merge review
chain.what_was_checked: Whether the defects could be removed at the cause rather than annotated, and whether the repair itself was sound.
chain.outcome: All gating claims confirmed and then removed at the cause: sharing-aware flattening added to the baseline, a memoised evaluator, and a proper CSE baseline. The merge review found further concerns, which were fixed in a final pass.

chain.stage: Corrected kernel experiment and consolidated erratum
chain.what_was_checked: Seven externally reported findings, and a rebuilt experiment on a balanced corpus with the repaired baseline.
chain.outcome: Six findings confirmed and addressed, one refuted on the evidence. The rebuilt experiment produced the current headline. The archived figure it replaced, and the retracted compression headline, were entered into a standing erratum.

chain.stage: Final acceptance review, then independent spot replication
chain.what_was_checked: Whether the corrective pass was ready for outside review; then, by a third party, whether every summary statistic could be reproduced from the raw rows.
chain.outcome: Accepted, then INDEPENDENT REAGGREGATION PASSED. The corpus regenerates byte-identically under different hash seeds; every summary row reproduced to floating-point tolerance; break-even reproduced exactly on every formula; all stratified intervals agreed.

chain.stage: Post-acceptance optimisation decision — kernel equivalence declared provisional
chain.what_was_checked: Given the accepted evidence, what to optimise next — and what not to.
chain.outcome: Kernel equivalence with a flattened CSE selected as the operating posture, explicitly PROVISIONAL pending the external campaign. Kernel work on the residual rejected as below the materiality bar. Priorities moved to preparation cost, cache behaviour and backend selection.

chain.stage: Benchmark refresh, local legs — replay, wrapper boundary, compile scaling, guard sweep
chain.what_was_checked: Whether the headline replays; where the whole-call boundary actually sits; whether compilation tracks the shared graph; whether the guard is ever wrong.
chain.outcome: Replay confirmed with identity fields exact. Wrapper claim REVISED — the earlier “CM ahead at 12 and 16” did not survive. Compile scaling confirmed. Guard confirmed with {{guard.wrong}} wrong decisions in {{guard.trials}} trials.

chain.stage: Matched decision-diagram comparison on a Linux machine
chain.what_was_checked: Construction and extraction costs against the packed kernels, on the same box, with full extraction equality rather than sampled checks.
chain.outcome: Confirmed with matched-cost evidence that a prior audit had been unable to obtain. Correctness gates held on all {{cudd.rows}} rows.
