glossary.lay: A rule that takes a set of yes/no inputs and produces a single yes/no answer. “Is this person allowed in?” given whether they are staff, whether their pass is valid, and whether it is out of hours.
glossary.technical: A mapping from {0,1}ⁿ to {0,1}. Everything on this site is about representing, evaluating and comparing such mappings.

glossary.lay: A complete list: every possible combination of inputs, and the answer for each. It says nothing about how the answer is produced — only what it is.
glossary.technical: The explicit enumeration of a Boolean function's outputs over all 2ⁿ input assignments, under a fixed variable ordering. Complete, canonical for that ordering, and exponential in size.

glossary.lay: The sequence in which you consider the inputs. It makes no difference to the answer, but for some representations it makes an enormous difference to how big the representation is.
glossary.technical: A total order on the variable set. Decision diagrams are canonical only with respect to a fixed order, and their size can vary from linear to exponential across orders for the same function.

glossary.lay: A standard way of writing something down such that two things that mean the same thing look identical. Once you have it, checking sameness is just checking whether the two look alike.
glossary.technical: A representation with the property that semantically equivalent objects map to syntactically identical artifacts under fixed conventions. Reduces equivalence checking to identity comparison.

glossary.lay: Proving that two differently written rules always give the same answer — for every possible input, not just the ones you tried.
glossary.technical: Deciding whether two Boolean functions are identical. Approaches differ fundamentally: compare complete outputs, compare canonical graphs in a shared manager, or prove the difference unsatisfiable.

glossary.lay: The question “is there any way at all to make this come out true?” Answering it does not require listing every possibility — good solvers find one answer, or prove none exists, without enumerating.
glossary.technical: The decision problem for existence of a satisfying assignment. An existential question, distinct from the exhaustive-enumeration questions the evaluators on this site answer.

glossary.lay: What is left of a rule once you fix one of its inputs. Fix “is staff = yes” and you get a simpler rule about everything else.
glossary.technical: The restriction of a function obtained by fixing one variable to a constant. The basic operation underlying decision-diagram construction and partial evaluation.

glossary.lay: A way of writing a circuit using only two-input ANDs and inverters. Restrictive, but it makes a lot of automated reasoning simpler, so it is a common exchange format for real designs.
glossary.technical: An And-Inverter Graph: a DAG of two-input AND nodes with optional edge complementation. The format of the external benchmark circuits used on this site.

glossary.lay: One output of a circuit, together with everything feeding into it. Circuits have many outputs; a cone is the self-contained rule behind one of them.
glossary.technical: The transitive fan-in of a single output in a combinational network. The external corpus is built from cones admitted by semantic-support bounds.

glossary.lay: Rewriting a rule as a short list of “all of these at once” groups joined by OR — and making that list as short as possible. It is what you want if the next step is turning the rule into physical gates.
glossary.technical: Minimisation to sum-of-products form. The AND-groups are called product terms or implicants; the dual form, OR-groups joined by AND, is the one whose groups are called clauses. Optimises expression size, not evaluation speed.

glossary.lay: Noticing that the same sub-calculation appears several times and doing it only once. The workhorse optimisation behind every compiled evaluator here, and the baseline CM has to beat.
glossary.technical: Rewriting an expression tree into a shared DAG so structurally identical subexpressions become a single node, typically by hash-consing. Evaluated once per node rather than once per occurrence.

glossary.lay: Giving every distinct piece of an expression a fingerprint, and keeping only one copy of each. If you build the same piece twice, you get the same object back rather than a duplicate.
glossary.technical: Interning structurally identical subterms via a hash table keyed on the node's constructor and children, so structural equality becomes pointer equality. The mechanism underlying both CSE and CM's canonical keys.

glossary.lay: Collapsing a chain of the same operation into one wide operation — but only where doing so does not force you to redo work you were already sharing. Adding this to the baseline is what closed most of CM's apparent kernel advantage.
glossary.technical: n-ary flattening of associative operator chains that respects the shared DAG, avoiding the duplication a naive flatten introduces at shared nodes. Its absence from an earlier baseline is the cause of a retracted headline in this project's history.

glossary.lay: Turning “A and B, then and C, then and D” into a single “and all four of these”. Fewer, wider steps. This is the entire mechanism behind CM's measured kernel advantage over an unflattened baseline.
glossary.technical: Emitting one wide instruction for an associative operator chain instead of one instruction per binary application. Predicts parity on corpora with no mergeable chains — which is exactly what the AND/INV external corpus showed.

glossary.lay: The same expression can be drawn as a tree, where every repeated piece is written out again, or as a graph, where repeats point back to one copy. The tree can be astronomically bigger for the same rule.
glossary.technical: The sharing factor is unfolded occurrences divided by structural DAG nodes. Compilation cost tracking DAG nodes rather than unfolded occurrences is what makes highly shared expressions cheap to compile.

glossary.lay: Instead of working out the answer for one input combination at a time, pack many combinations into a single machine word and compute them all at once with one instruction.
glossary.technical: Evaluating a Boolean function over many assignments simultaneously by packing assignment bits into machine words and applying bitwise operations. The output remains exponential in semantic support.

glossary.lay: Two ways to hold the packed bits: as a list of machine-sized chunks, or as one arbitrarily large number. Chunks are faster once there is enough work; the big number wins when there is not, because it has less setup.
glossary.technical: The words engine operates over arrays of fixed-width words with a fixed dispatch cost; the bigint engines operate over Python arbitrary-precision integers. Which is faster is an amortisation question, not a fixed variable-count threshold.

glossary.lay: The plain packed-bit executor: it computes the whole answer table using ordinary bitwise instructions and essentially no setup. It is the comparison arm CM has to beat at the whole-call boundary, and it wins at every size measured here.
glossary.technical: The bare packed kernel used as the wrapper-boundary baseline. No structural artifact, no cache, no canonical key — and correspondingly no overhead to amortise.

glossary.lay: A Boolean operator written as an ordered grid of bits, treated as an object in its own right rather than as a list of answers.
glossary.technical: An ordered binary matrix representation of a Boolean operator. Uniqueness is relative to an ordered variable basis; matrix equality requires the same normalised ordered basis on both sides.

glossary.lay: A second matrix form built under a different construction convention. It expresses the same things a CM does, written a different way.
glossary.technical: A related matrix representation in the CM family, distinguished by its construction convention rather than by what it can express.

glossary.lay: The fully written-out matrix. Only built when the matrix itself is what you asked for — it grows exponentially with the number of variables that matter.
glossary.technical: The materialised CM matrix, exponential in semantic support. Not the artifact produced on the packed evaluation path, and not optimised for raw execution speed.

glossary.lay: Producing the packed answer without ever building the full matrix along the way. Building it and then throwing it away would cost far more than the answer is worth.
glossary.technical: The CM execution path that emits reduced packed output directly, skipping dense matrix materialisation when the requested artifact is a truth vector.

glossary.lay: The internal form a system compiles your expression into before running it — not what you wrote, and not the final answer, but the working form in between.
glossary.technical: CM's structural IR is a shared DAG over interned nodes, from which an executable instruction program is lowered.

glossary.lay: A fingerprint of the compiled form, used to remember what has already been built so an identical expression can reuse it instead of being compiled again.
glossary.technical: A digest-keyed cache of compiled structural IR, returning one object per digest. Its steady-state hit rate and size sensitivity under realistic mixes are unmeasured — one of the named open items.

glossary.lay: The agreed sequence of variables that a matrix is written relative to. Two matrices only mean the same thing if they were written against the same sequence.
glossary.technical: The ordered variable basis defining CM uniqueness. Basis-normalised comparison is a precondition for any matrix-equality claim.

glossary.lay: Reading one specific fact out of the matrix by multiplying it against a pair of pick-one-thing vectors — the equivalent of asking the operator a single question instead of unpacking all of its answers.
glossary.technical: Logical measurement using ordered bra and ket vectors against the CM. Present in the formalism; its practical performance advantage has not been benchmarked.

glossary.lay: A compressed decision tree with all duplicate branches merged. For a fixed variable order it is canonical: two functions are the same exactly when their graphs are the same.
glossary.technical: Reduced Ordered Binary Decision Diagram. Canonical under a fixed variable order; size is order-sensitive, and extracting an explicit truth vector requires one traversal per assignment.

glossary.lay: The widely used library that implements decision diagrams. When this site says “CUDD”, it means measurements made with the real native library, not a re-implementation.
glossary.technical: The Colorado University Decision Diagram package, used natively. Every measured row carries a flag confirming the native library was in use, and full-extraction equality against the packed bits was verified on every row.

glossary.lay: Building a decision diagram using one prescribed variable order, without searching for a better one.
glossary.technical: A single build under a prescribed natural order, with no order search and no dynamic reordering. The convention used for the matched cost comparison.

glossary.lay: The build time of whichever attempt a search decided to keep. Importantly, that is not necessarily the fastest attempt — it is the one that produced the smallest graph.
glossary.technical: The build interval of the trial retained by the configured selection objective, which prioritises node count and only then build time. Quoting it without the search total understates the true cost.

glossary.lay: The full cost of trying several variable orders and keeping the best. It is the honest figure to quote if you searched, because you paid for every attempt, not just the winner.
glossary.technical: The summed cost of all trial builds in a best-of-k order search. On this site it is reported beside the single-build cost and never omitted.

glossary.lay: A decision-diagram library rearranging its own variable order automatically when the graph grows too large. On the graphs measured here it never activated, because they never got big enough to trigger it.
glossary.technical: Automatic variable-reordering triggered by node-count growth thresholds. Node ratio was exactly {{bx2.reorder_ratio}} across all strata here, which characterises this corpus as small for the library rather than characterising reordering.

glossary.lay: How many variables exist in the surrounding system. Not a measure of how big the job is — most of them may be irrelevant to the expression at hand.
glossary.technical: The size of the variable namespace. Measured here to be irrelevant to cost at fixed semantic support.

glossary.lay: The variables that literally appear in the expression as written. Some of them may still have no effect on the answer.
glossary.technical: Variables occurring in the expression's syntax. An upper bound on semantic support, not equal to it.

glossary.lay: How many variables actually change the answer. This is the honest measure of how big a job is, and it is the horizontal axis of nearly every chart here.
glossary.technical: The number of variables the function genuinely depends on, measured rather than assumed. Explicit output size is 2^live_k. A variable can appear syntactically and be semantically dead.

glossary.lay: The system declining to produce an explicit answer table because it would be too large. A deliberate refusal, recorded as such, not a failure.
glossary.technical: An intentional refusal above the explicit-output guard at live_k={{guard.k}}. Skips are counted and reported; across {{guard.trials}} fresh trials there were {{guard.wrong}} incorrect guard decisions and {{guard.oversized}} oversized outputs.

glossary.lay: The whole end-to-end call: everything from handing over your inputs to getting the answer back, including all the bookkeeping in between — not just the computation itself.
glossary.technical: The full call path including argument binding, environment setup, cache lookup, kernel execution and result extraction. Distinguished throughout from the kernel.

glossary.lay: The computation proper, with the setup and teardown stripped away. Two systems can have identical kernels and very different end-to-end costs.
glossary.technical: The steady-state execution of the compiled program with environment and program prebuilt. At this boundary CM/CSE-flat measured parity on B1/E3 and EPFL, but a workload-specific CM advantage on current B2/B4 V3.

glossary.lay: The difference between the end-to-end call and the computation proper — the fixed price of using the system at all. Roughly constant, which is why it dominates when the actual work is small.
glossary.technical: End-to-end call time minus kernel time, {{wrap.ovh.min}}–{{wrap.ovh.max}} median on the current corpus and protocol. Not separable at the smallest stratum, where the fallback engine is used.

glossary.lay: The one-time cost of compiling an expression before you can evaluate it. The prep multiple is that cost expressed as a ratio against a named baseline — and the baseline must always be named, because it changes the number.
glossary.technical: Compilation cost, linear in structural DAG nodes. Geometric-mean multiple against plain CSE and against CSE-flat differ and are never interchanged. It is now profiled, has one accepted memo-reduction improvement, and remains the top-ranked optimisation surface.

glossary.lay: Running an expression that has already been compiled and bound, so the setup is not paid again.
glossary.technical: Execution after binding preparation is complete. Preparation is a separate one-time cost and is never folded into the per-call figure.

glossary.lay: How many times you must evaluate the same expression before the compilation cost is repaid. Below it you lose; above it you win. It is the single most useful number to know about your workload.
glossary.technical: Preparation premium divided by per-evaluation kernel gain. A formula is classified never-break-even exactly when that gain is not positive — preparation cost sets the magnitude of finite counts but plays no part in the classification.

glossary.lay: One timing of the same expression under two different methods, so the comparison is like-for-like. Only pairs where both methods succeeded are counted.
glossary.technical: A matched measurement across arms for one formula. Unmatched observations are excluded from ratio aggregation to avoid survivorship bias.

glossary.lay: One of the methods being compared in an experiment. Saying “CM was 10% faster” is meaningless without saying faster than which arm.
glossary.technical: A measurement condition in a paired comparison — here CM, plain CSE, CSE-flat, BitSet, or a decision diagram. Every ratio on this site names both arms.

glossary.lay: The set of distinct expressions in a group. Timing one expression seven times gives you seven measurements but still only one expression.
glossary.technical: The set of distinct formulas in a stratum — the inferential unit. An earlier pass in this project discovered that a controlled stratum contained one formula re-bound several ways, making the effective sample size one.

glossary.lay: Take the typical time for each method, then divide. Different from taking each pair's ratio and finding the typical one — the two can disagree, so which was used is always stated.
glossary.technical: median(A) ÷ median(B) across a stratum's observations. Distinct from the median paired ratio; both appear on this site and each is labelled.

glossary.lay: Work out the ratio for each expression individually, then take the typical one. More robust to one expression being unusual than dividing the two typical times.
glossary.technical: The median of per-observation A÷B ratios. Preferred where formula-to-formula variation is large.

glossary.lay: Exactly what a stopwatch reading includes. Setup? Extraction? Both? Every figure here says which, because comparing an inclusive figure to an exclusive one is the easiest way to publish a wrong ratio.
glossary.technical: The labelled timing boundary: prep, kernel, end-to-end call, extraction, build. Build-window conventions that differ between runs are stated and never plotted on a shared axis.

glossary.lay: The right kind of average for ratios. If one measurement says “twice as fast” and another says “half as fast”, an ordinary average says 1.25 — which is wrong. The geometric mean correctly says 1.
glossary.technical: The exponential of the mean of the logs. Used for all ratio aggregation here because ratios are multiplicative and their distribution is skewed in linear space.

glossary.lay: A way of asking “how much would this number move if I had happened to test a different sample?” — by repeatedly re-drawing from the data you have and watching how far the answer wanders.
glossary.technical: A resampling interval. The resampling unit is the crucial choice: resample the wrong unit and the interval is meaningless regardless of how many draws you take.

glossary.lay: Re-drawing whole groups rather than individual measurements, when the measurements inside a group are related. Cones from one circuit are not independent, so whole circuits are re-drawn.
glossary.technical: Resampling at the cluster level — circuit, cell, or machine. Produces wider and more honest intervals than naive resampling when within-cluster correlation exists.

glossary.lay: The error of counting repeated measurements of the same thing as if they were measurements of different things. It makes error bars look far tighter than they are, and can turn ordinary noise into an apparently solid finding.
glossary.technical: Treating within-unit repeated measures as independent observations, inflating effective sample size and understating variance. The specific failure clustered intervals exist to prevent.

glossary.lay: Roughly, how much independent information your data actually contains after accounting for everything you estimated from it. Getting it wrong makes your spread estimate too small.
glossary.technical: Residual degrees of freedom after estimating cell means. An earlier pass in this project divided a residual sum of squares by the raw observation count rather than the residual degrees of freedom, understating the spread estimate; units in singleton cells contribute no residual information.

glossary.lay: Timing all of one method, then all of the other. Each method gets a run where the data it needs is likely still sitting in the computer's fast temporary memory.
glossary.technical: All measurements of one arm, then all of the next. Reported as its own column and never pooled with the alternating order.

glossary.lay: Alternating between the methods, one after another. This keeps the two on a more even footing over time, but each one is more likely to find the computer's fast memory holding the other method's data.
glossary.technical: Interleaved measurement across arms. Stresses cache and CPU state differently from the blocked order; agreement between the two is reported, not assumed.

glossary.lay: Writing down what you are going to measure and what would count as a positive result — before you have the data. It is what makes a negative result meaningful rather than merely disappointing.
glossary.technical: Fixing corpus source, selection rules, arms, schedules, clustering basis and decision thresholds in a frozen protocol before any measurement exists.

glossary.lay: The pass mark, agreed in advance: how big an effect would have to be, and how confident you would have to be about it, before it is worth acting on. On the decisive experiment here, the pass mark was not met.
glossary.technical: A conjunction of pre-registered conditions — an effect-size threshold, an interval excluding parity, and a break-even bound — all of which must hold for optimisation to be warranted. Its failure is what made the kernel-equivalence posture final.

glossary.lay: The check that runs before any timing: every method must produce exactly the same answer bits. Fail it and the run stops rather than producing a number.
glossary.technical: Bit-for-bit output agreement across all arms as a precondition for measurement. Strengthened to full-extraction equality rather than sampled checks for the decision-diagram comparison.

glossary.lay: Having a second, separate piece of code recompute every headline number from the individual measurements — so a bug in the summariser cannot become a published result.
glossary.technical: Recomputation of every summary statistic from raw per-formula rows by a pass independent of the driver. Required before citation; performed again by this page's build script.

glossary.lay: Judging a method only on the cases it managed to finish. If it gives up on the hard ones and its rival does not, it will look faster than it is.
glossary.technical: Aggregation over unmatched observations, where one arm's failures are silently excluded. Prevented by failure-aware paired reporting: only matched pairs are aggregated and every refusal is counted.

glossary.lay: Formally retiring a published number — recording that it is withdrawn, why, and what replaced it — instead of quietly deleting it. Anyone who read the old version can find out exactly what changed.
glossary.technical: A standing erratum and claim map assigning each prior claim a status of confirmed, revised or superseded with its replacement. Superseded figures appear on this site only in the corrections ledger and are never plotted.

glossary.lay: A published, freely available collection of real hardware circuit designs, widely used for comparing logic tools. Using it means testing against something the project did not choose or shape.
glossary.technical: The external combinational benchmark suite from which {{epfl.n_cones}} AND/INV cones across {{epfl.n_circuits}} circuits were extracted, at a pinned upstream commit with per-file digests recorded.

glossary.lay: The parts of a benchmark row that say which expression it is, as opposed to how fast it ran. If those match exactly between two runs, you know both runs asked the same questions.
glossary.technical: Non-timing row fields — formula id, truth digest, support, structural counts. Exact match across runs establishes that a difference is timing, not workload.

glossary.lay: A cheap check that runs before the expensive work and stops everything if it fails — such as a small pilot run, or verifying the test set's fingerprint.
glossary.technical: A deterministic pilot plus a pre-registered runtime bound before each full run, alongside corpus digest verification and truth-digest re-verification at measurement time.
